blocks.text: “Thanks, and thanks, and thanks again for your sweet letter. It was so nice to be able to tell you and to have your sympathy.

“My dear, when one thing happens, everything seems to happen at once. How true the old sayings are. I will be twenty in September, and I never had a marriage proposal until today—not a real one. Yet today I have had three! Just imagine! THREE proposals in one day! Isn’t it awful! I feel sorry, really and truly sorry, for two of the poor men. Oh, Mina, I am so happy that I don’t know what to do with myself. And three proposals! But please, don’t tell any of the girls. They would get all sorts of wild ideas. They would imagine they were hurt and insulted if they did not get at least six proposals on their very first day at home. Some girls think far too much of themselves! You and I, Mina dear, are engaged. We are soon going to settle down quietly and seriously as old married women. So we can look down on such foolish pride. Well, I must tell you about the three men. But you must keep it a secret from everyone, dear—except Jonathan, of course. You will tell him, because if I were in your place, I would certainly tell Arthur. A woman should tell her husband everything—don’t you think so, dear?—and I must be fair. Men want women, and especially their wives, to be just as fair as men are. And I am afraid women are not always as fair as they should be. Well, my dear, number One came just before lunch. I told you about him—Dr. John Seward, the man from the mental hospital, with the strong jaw and the good forehead. He looked very calm on the outside, but he was nervous all the same. He had clearly been practicing all sorts of little details, and he remembered them. Even so, he almost sat down on his silk hat. Men do not usually do that when they are calm. Then, when he wanted to look relaxed, he kept playing with a small medical knife in a way that almost made me scream. He spoke to me very directly and honestly, Mina. He told me how much I meant to him, even though he had known me for such a short time. He also told me what his life would be like with me there to help and cheer him. He was going to tell me how unhappy he would be if I did not care for him. But when he saw me cry, he called himself a cruel man and said he would not add to my present trouble. Then he stopped and asked if I could love him in time. When I shook my head, his hands shook. Then he hesitated and asked if I already cared for someone else. He asked very kindly. He said he did not want to force my secret out of me. He only wanted to know, because if a woman’s heart was free, a man might have hope. And then, Mina, I felt a kind of duty to tell him that there was someone. I only told him that much. Then he stood up. He looked very strong and very serious as he took both of my hands in his. He said he hoped I would be happy, and that if I ever needed a friend, I must think of him as one of my best. Oh, Mina dear, I can’t help crying, and you must excuse how smudged this letter is. Being proposed to is all very nice and all that. But it is not a happy thing at all to see a poor man walk away looking completely heartbroken, when you know he truly loves you. And you know that, no matter what he says at the moment, you are leaving his life completely. My dear, I must stop here for now. I feel so miserable, even though I am so happy.

“Arthur has just left, and I feel in a better mood than when I stopped writing. So I can go on telling you about the day. Well, my dear, number Two came after lunch. He is such a nice man, an American from Texas. He looks so young and fresh that it seems almost impossible he has been to so many places and had such adventures. I understand how poor Desdemona felt when such a dangerous stream was poured into her ear, even by a black man. I suppose we women are such cowards that we think a man will save us from our fears, so we marry him. Now I know what I would do if I were a man and wanted to make a girl love me. No, I don’t! Mr. Morris was telling us his stories, and Arthur never told any, and yet— My dear, I am getting ahead of myself. Mr. Quincey P. Morris found me alone. It seems that a man always manages to find a girl alone. No, that isn’t true! Arthur tried twice to make a chance, and I helped him as much as I could. I am not ashamed to say so now. I must tell you first that Mr. Morris does not always use slang. He never speaks that way to strangers or in front of them. He is really well educated and has wonderful manners. However, he discovered that it amused me to hear him use American slang. So whenever I was there, and no one around would be shocked, he said such funny things. I am afraid, my dear, that he has to make it all up, because it fits so perfectly with everything else he says. Still, that is just the way slang works. I do not know if I will ever use slang myself. I do not know if Arthur likes it, because I have never heard him use any yet. Well, Mr. Morris sat down beside me and tried to look as happy and cheerful as he could. All the same, I could see that he was very nervous. He took my hand in his and said so very sweetly:—
